cells.tense: You are standing in the calm the change left behind, and it is holding.
cells.ask: Ask one person for their fair share of what you keep steady, with a number or a date on it, and keep what they say.
cells.core:
When the change settled, you kept what it made. You didn't tear it up or move on too fast — you held it steady, and it's holding. The pull toward what you want and the form you keep are in the same room, which is rarer than it sounds. That's what going well looks like here: you know which direction matters to you and you don't have to force it, because the ground under you is already solid.

That solidity is what lets fair exchange keep running. You know what's yours to give and what's yours to get back, and you're not counting it constantly. So ask one person for their fair share of what you keep steady, and keep what they say.

cells.tense: You will have every version of how this works held in place, and none of them is here yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're stabilizing and leave it alone for a week except for what today needs.
cells.core:
You're getting ahead of the change. The work you did is done, but you're still reinforcing it — testing the ends, bracing for the next turn, gripping the whole thing in a hand that's already tight. From outside it looks like care. It's worry doing the work.

What going well looks like here is simpler and quieter: you follow what pulls you without checking whether the ground will hold, because you can feel that it does. Instead you are bracing so far ahead that the pull toward what you actually want goes faint under all the gripping. Pick one thing you're stabilizing and leave it alone for a week except for what today needs. Let the form prove it can stand.

cells.tense: You stood at a door that was already behind you, and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Take one small stretch back toward a thing you stopped doing, and do it today before the hour is chosen for you.
cells.core:
The change got made, and you haven't moved in with what it made. Something closed and you're still facing that way — you kept the shape of what came out of it, but you haven't stepped into any of it. The pull toward what you want didn't disappear. You just stopped walking toward it.

What going well looks like here is heading for one thing on purpose and letting that direction set your day. That's the missing piece — not keeping things steady, but moving. Take one small stretch back toward a thing you stopped doing, and do it today. It doesn't have to be big; it has to move.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what gets kept around you, and you talk about it as if it just happens.
cells.ask: Name one thing you kept standing these past months that would have fallen without you — and say it as yours.
cells.core:
Look at what's steady around you and ask who made it steady. You did. The people who count on things staying where they are, the routines that hold this whole stretch together — you're the one keeping them. But when you describe it, you talk like it's just how the place runs.

What going well looks like here is calling the direction your own out loud, so what orients you is a thing you chose instead of a current you happen to be in. You're not holding back from taking credit. You've just been inside the scaffold, looking at it from within. Name one thing you kept standing these past months that would have fallen without you. Say it as yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft is that a past ending or loss sits behind the person's quiet — the record says only that the offering stopped, not when, who, or what it cost, so I keep that cell at mechanism-only. A reader could reasonably say the steadiness after change is just what their nature does now, so each core leans on the mechanism rather than their history and leaves them a way to say no. The asks survive being wrong because each one is a plain act — ask a fair share, tell a person, take one stretch back, keep a decision — useful on its own. The line that served me more than them was 'the still thing isn't the starting point' — and I cut it in favor of what goes on over months, not a flourish.
